paragraphs.source_en: “That is quite understandable,” said my master. Recalling his own position as a teacher of foreign languages, my master felt deep sympathy. Meitei went on: “Just then, however, idlers began gathering around, one by one, staring as though at some curiosity. In the end Tofu and the two Germans were surrounded on every side. The fellow went scarlet and stammered helplessly; compared with his proud air at the start, he was now in a truly pitiable state.” “And how did it all end?” asked my master. Meitei replied, “In the end Tofu seems to have been unable to bear it any longer; he said ‘sainara’ in Japanese and hurried back, shaking off the Germans. I asked him, ‘That “sainara” is rather odd. Is it your local dialect to say “sainara” instead of “sayonara”?’ He answered, ‘No, where I come from we say “sayonara” too, but since the other party was a Westerner, I said “sainara” in order to harmonize it with German.’ That Tofu is admirable: even in his extremity he never forgets harmony!” “Never mind whether it was sayonara or sainara. What happened to the Westerner?” “They say the Westerner was dumbfounded and stood there in a daze. Ha ha! Isn’t it funny?” “I do not see anything especially funny in it. What is far funnier is your coming all this way just to report such a trifle.” So saying, my master flicked the ash from his cigarette into the brazier. At that moment the bell on the lattice door outside rang with a startling clamor, and a woman’s shrill voice followed: “Excuse me, is anyone at home?” Meitei and my master involuntarily looked at each other, and neither said a word.

paragraphs.source_en: I thought, “How rare: a female visitor has come to my master’s house.” Looking closely, I saw that the owner of that shrill voice had entered, dragging the hem of her double-layered crepe finery over the mats. She was probably just past forty. From her receding hairline, her front hair rose up like an embankment, thrusting at least half the length of her face toward the heavens. Her eyes, like the slopes of a cutting, slanted sharply upward and faced one another left and right as two straight lines. By “straight lines,” I mean eyes even narrower and longer than a whale’s. Only her nose was absurdly large, as though someone else’s nose had been stolen and planted in the middle of her face. Her nose was like moving a stone lantern from Shokonsha into a little courtyard only a few yards square: it dominated everything, yet somehow seemed out of place. It was, moreover, a hook nose: it first made a fierce effort to rise as high as it could, then, as though deciding it had overdone things, became modest halfway along, lost its earlier vigor toward the tip, and drooped down to peer at the lip beneath. Because it was such a remarkably distinctive nose, whenever the woman spoke, one felt not so much that her mouth was speaking as that her nose was doing the talking. To show respect for this magnificent nose, I shall henceforth call the woman “Madam Nose.” After first exchanging the usual greetings, Madam Nose glanced coldly around my master’s parlor and said, “My, what a splendid residence you have!” My master thought, “Liar.” Then he went on puffing steadily at his cigarette. Looking up at the ceiling, Meitei said, “Kushami, is that a rain stain, or is it the grain of the boards? Look at it; what an interesting pattern!” Meitei was plainly trying, in an indirect way, to draw my master into speaking. My master answered, “What else could it be? It is a rain stain.” With a perfectly composed face, Meitei said, “Splendid.” Madam Nose was inwardly angry that these two men knew nothing of social manners. And so the three sat like the three legs of a tripod, silent for quite some time.

units.source_zh: 我想：“真稀奇，主人家居然来了女客。”
